paras: The attempted lynching of William Neal, Ellis Craft and George Ellis took place at Catlettsburg, Boyd County, Kentucky, in January 1882, when a large crowd gathered to lynch three white men jailed for the murders of two girls and a boy at nearby Ashland. On January 5 the sheriff took the prisoners down the river by ferry and steamer while the crowd seized the steamer Mountain Girl and gave chase, giving up only when state militia took charge of the prisoners. No one was hurt, the men were lodged in the Maysville jail that night, and within about a month Neal and Craft had been convicted and sentenced to death.

The three men were arrested on the strength of a confession by George Ellis, who said that he, Neal and Craft entered the Gibbons house at Ashland by a window, that Neal and Craft "outraged" the two girls, and that the girls, Fanny Gibbons and Emma Thomas, and the boy Robert were killed with an axe. According to an Ashland dispatch, the men were first held quietly at a hotel by Constable Heflin, and Neal also confessed before he and Ellis waived examination. The bodies were exhumed and the wounds were said to match Ellis's account, though Neal and Craft later claimed they could prove an alibi and Ellis said he had been forced to take part.

By January 3 crowds were gathering at Catlettsburg, where the men were jailed, and dispatches reported that "threats of lynching are common." On the night of January 4 the Adjutant General, by order of Governor Blackburn, directed the Mason County Guards at Maysville to go to Catlettsburg and report to Judge G. M. Brown to keep the peace, and the company left on the steamer Hudson early the next morning. The Maysville Daily Evening Bulletin reported that hundreds were flocking to the town, business was suspended and the prisoners were "in imminent danger of being lynched."

On the morning of January 5 Craft waived his preliminary examination at Catlettsburg as the crowd grew, and word came that a train of lynchers had left Ashland. Judge Brown then ordered the prisoners removed to the Maysville jail and adjourned the circuit court to January 16. The steamer Mountain Girl was chartered for the trip but had too little steam, and meanwhile, by one wire account, the Ashland train arrived with "about 500 determined Regulators." The wire account said Sheriff John Kounz and ten guards moved the prisoners from the jail to the wharf, while the Maysville Bulletin said they were taken to the court house as if for examination and out a back door to the river. When the crowd saw the prisoners it ran down the bank with loud yells, carrying arms and missiles, and the sheriff's party boarded a ferryboat and headed downstream.

Members of the crowd took over the Mountain Girl, cut her loose and followed, raising steam, the Maysville Bulletin said, by burning rosin. As the steamer closed on the slow ferry, the sheriff hailed the Mountain Boy, which was coming upriver on its regular run, transferred the prisoners and turned back downstream ahead of the pursuers. Ironton dispatches placed the transfer at the Sheridan coal works below Catlettsburg and reported that the Mountain Boy passed Ironton at 2 p.m., while the crowd left the Mountain Girl at Ashland to look for a train to head the boat off at Portsmouth. Near Riverton the Hudson met the Mountain Boy, Captain A. C. Respess's guards took charge of the prisoners, and those on the Mountain Girl abandoned the chase on learning that militia guarded them. At Portsmouth, where the boat stopped for coal, the troops had difficulty keeping people from boarding, and the prisoners were lodged in the Maysville jail at about 10 p.m.

Back at Catlettsburg, the Ashland men turned their anger on Judge Brown: an indignation meeting resolved to bring the prisoners back and protect them until trial, and a committee asked him to rescind his order, which he refused. One report said two other judges were threatened and stayed indoors. A mass meeting asked the legislature for a special court, and on January 9 a grand jury was impanelled at Catlettsburg under a special act, with John Russell of the Ashland Citizens' Committee as foreman. The Catlettsburg correspondent wrote that there would be no interference while the law took its course, but "if another attempt is made to remove the prisoners it will be hard to restrain the fury of the people."

On February 6, with three militia companies in the courtroom, Judge Brown sentenced Neal to hang on April 14 and thanked the Mason County Guards for coming to the aid of the law. Neal protested his innocence, Craft was to be sentenced the next day, and Ellis's trial was put off to the next term. No report of arrests among the pursuers appears in the coverage.

The case traveled widely by wire: the confession and lynching threats ran on January 4 and 5 in papers from the Daily Kennebec Journal to the Salt Lake Herald and the Savannah Morning News, and the chase appeared on January 6 in papers from Sacramento to Wheeling, St. Paul and Knoxville. Headlines treated the episode as a chase, among them "A Sheriff's Race for Life With His Prisoners," "THE MAD MOB" and "LYNCHERS FOILED." The same reports called the prisoners "the Ashland fiends" and "the murderers" before any trial.

Delaware's Daily Republican, in an aside, described Kentucky's way of punishing criminals as "not strictly in accordance with the law" but a saving of trials and expense. The Maysville Bulletin, nearest to events, printed the militia order with the names of the guardsmen and called the prisoners "bad looking men and of a brutal type." A month later the Bulletin described the crowd as "one of the largest that ever gathered in the state" and offered the quick convictions as proof of "prompter and more efficient administration of the law."

Estimates of the crowd ranged from about 200 in one version of the Ironton dispatch, to 450 in a Lancaster report and about 500 on the Ashland train, to about 2,000 in another version of the same dispatch and in the Maysville Bulletin. An Ashland special claimed the men had come to Catlettsburg to protect the prisoners and see that they got a fair trial, while the other reports, including the Maysville Bulletin, said the crowd gathered to lynch them. Most accounts credit Judge Brown with the removal order, but one dispatch said the sheriff moved the men secretly and a Delaware paper attributed it to the governor.

The Dallas Weekly Herald reported a jury verdict against "Ellis and Craft," but the more detailed Catlettsburg special said Ellis's trial had been postponed, and the Maysville Bulletin counted two men convicted.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd gathered at Catlettsburg to lynch three jailed murder suspects and chased the sheriff's boat down the river, but never reached them (A1, A8, A11).

A crowd of hundreds or more, acting without authority over a murder accusation, pursued the prisoners to lynch them, but the sheriff and militia got them to the Maysville jail and no one was killed (A8, A10, A11).

Several independent dispatches (Catlettsburg, Ironton, Ashland, Portsmouth) and the Maysville Bulletin's own account agree on the gathering, the removal by boat and the steamer chase (A8, A9, A10, A11, A14).
